Additionally, we develop a closure theorem for its associated second-order cone relaxation.

This paper focuses on deriving a comprehensive description of the general form
for generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan derivations in the context of a semiprime ring $R$.
It is demonstrated that if the ring $R$ is semiprime, $\sigma$ is an automorphism, and $F(R)$
is the skew field of $R$, then any generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan derivation $\Delta$ in $R$
is expressible as $d +\phi\sigma^{-n}$, where $d$ is a derivation in $R$, $\phi$ is an element
of $F(R)$, and the condition $n \leq m$ holds.

We are going to outline a comprehensive method, referred to as the "factorized CDMSS framework," capable of effectively organizing the effective field theory for compactified D-branes with space-time supersymmetry. This method breaks down the effective field theory into fundamental components, which are compactified down to three dimensions, and further categorizes these components based on their mass dimensions. The resulting theory can be expressed through generalized vertex operators, which are in turn connected through specific rules governing their connections, derived from the initial higher-dimensional theory. The method also allows us to explicitly define the terms in the CDMSS effective field theory, up to a specified level of complexity, by recursively applying the rules governing vertex interactions.

To investigate the decay rates for a nonlinear version of the Favard length that preserves asymptotic symmetry, we introduce two new sequences called $\left(\kappa_k,\lambda_k\right)$ which are derived from the heat kernel and an optimization problem. Our findings involve the complete identification of the set of potential $\lambda_k$ values that lead to standard or slow decay, as well as explicit examples of $\kappa_k$ profiles corresponding to each case. Furthermore, we establish a connection between our work and the linear decay phenomenon in convolution, and we provide an alternative proof of a existing theorem on the sharp bound for the Favard length in Riemannian manifolds.

To address limitations in traditional Model Predictive Control (MPC) due to constraints and adversarial disturbances, we present a Robust Tube variant, referred to as Robust Tube MPC, which ensures feasibility and constraint satisfaction even when faced with adverse disturbances. Building on the concept of Bellman cost, a new measure called Robust Bellman Cost is introduced to quantify the value of a Robust Tube. By leveraging the dynamic programming approach, the Robust Bellman Cost is computed in a computationally efficient manner. Notably, the Robust Tube MPC is an instance of the Generalized Model Predictive Control (GMPC) framework and is shown to be a special case of the well-established Sampling-Based MPC (SB-MPC) method. Furthermore, the Robust Tube is also explored as a means to enforce adversarial constraints and is demonstrated to achieve similar performance to SB-MPC under adversarial disturbances.

In a specific type of ferromagnetism, known as the nematic Heisenberg model, we have discovered a distinct anomaly in Hall resistance that changes with field orientation, occurring through a process called the intrinsic anomalous Hall effect. The cause of this phenomenon is a type of Berry curvature known as the second-order field-dependent Berry curvature. Our research reveals that, in the materials with the characteristics of $|\Delta \gamma_{xy} \sigma_{xy}| \sim bB^2$ with $b$ being a material-specific constant and $\sigma_{xy}$ being connected to the Hall conductivity, we can explain this anomaly. The materials with the characteristics of $|\Delta \gamma_{xy} \sigma_{xy}| \sim bB^2$ have a type of Berry curvature known as the second-order field-dependent Berry curvature. The cause of this phenomenon is a mixing of spin and orbital in the materials with the characteristics of $|\Delta \gamma_{xy} \sigma_{xy}| \sim bB^2$.

Visual analysis of parallel code focuses on understanding data distribution and assignment. Research has employed various methods to represent assignment and data distributions through parallel call graphs, which show how data is passed and received. However, efficiently scaling these visualizations for large code is crucial since long call chains obscure data distribution views. This paper presents ensemble-Sankey visualizations, which utilize multiple parallel call graph views in an interactive system to improve data distribution understanding for large-scale parallel codes. Ensemble-Sankey offers multiple perspectives through a Sankey-based interface that supports fast data navigation and distribution comparison. It integrates with an interface for examining code details and integrates with other visualization tools for comprehensive examination. A case study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in understanding data distribution and its implications on parallel code behavior.

A rapidly changing world is reflected in the continuous update of online news datasets. However, this causes problems for pre-trained language models (PLMs) that learn from outdated sources, resulting in a knowledge gap. To address these issues, a novel training strategy called EVPLM is proposed, which utilizes an incremental learning framework. Specifically, EVPLM employs a sliding window approach and a knowledge distillation technique to update the model's parameters using new data and gradually eliminate outdated information. Experimental results on both open and closed sets show that EVPLM outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods by a large margin.

Research has identified quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) in several solar and stellar objects. Despite efforts to model their dynamics, the physics behind these pulsations remains unclear. This study focuses on a specific type of solar flare observed on November 01, 2016, at 03:27:33 UT, in an active region near the solar limb. Analyzing the flare using various magnetohydrodynamics equations revealed that the QPPs could be caused by either a turbulent or dynamic photospheric current sheet. Furthermore, the study suggests that the QPPs' frequency modulation may be indicative of a resonant system. Resonance models based on magnetohydrodynamics equations were developed to simulate the QPPs, successfully reproducing their behavior.

This research introduces an anomaly detection method that can effectively identify anomalies in a variety of images. Our approach combines a conventional anomaly detection network with a customized loss function, while experimenting with distinct aggregation functions to analyze the output patterns of multiple convolutional layers. The proposed algorithm was evaluated using the CUB200-2011, PASCAL VOC 2012, and iNaturalist 2018 datasets, with our implementation available on the GitHub platform.

This study investigates the well-posedness of a range of high-order variants of the Kadomtsev–Petviashvili I equation in the space $H^{s_0}(\mathbb{R})$ with $s_0$ between $1/2$ and $3/4$. The paper demonstrates that the equation remains well-posed within this space, which is notable given that lower boundedness is achieved despite the equation being dispersive. Notably, previous results had only shown this type of well-posedness for initial data with zero values at infinity.

Kramer's theorem dictates that a collection of fermions at zero temperature will have a unique many-body ground state if each fermion has a separate potential well with a unique energy, even if the ground state is non-degenerate for individual particles. This rule has been broken in a system where particles interact through an attractive force, leading to a specific type of potential known as a Fano-Feschbach potential. This potential results in a type of two-body interaction that is zero at a specific distance. Our research has found that by adjusting this potential, multiple energy levels can be created in the many-body system's ground state. This breakthrough has implications for our understanding of ultracold atoms and photons, where these systems can be simulated using these potential interactions.

A novel prediction framework is introduced to accurately forecast channel behavior in complex MIMO systems by integrating deep learning techniques and historical channel data. The approach mirrors that of neural weather forecasting, predicting future conditions based on known environmental parameters. The proposed method excels in mass-market deployment scenarios where user mobility is high and data collection is limited. Two distinct scenarios are considered - the first, where a central base station has access to channel data from multiple users, and the second, where the base station can predict channels for a single user using collected data from that user. To optimize performance, a unique data representation is employed that combines spatial and temporal features. The proposed method demonstrates significant improvements over existing channel prediction models, particularly in terms of root mean square error and spectral delay spread.

This study develops novel estimators to determine regional income disparities, achieving accurate predictions at specific micro-regional locations through the application of quantile regression techniques. Specifically, two methods are proposed: the first employs a multivariate location-scale mixture model in combination with maximum likelihood estimation, while the second leverages a Bayesian approach using Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms. Through simulated data analysis, the validity of these new estimators is established, and an empirical application is conducted to measure the inequality of household incomes in Spain's 4091 micro-regions in 2015.

Given a real analytic manifold $M$ and an interval $I$ with $0$ as an interior point, we focus on the Grauert tube $\Pi(M, t)$ for $t > I$. We establish a formula for the Szegö projector on the Grauert tube using the strict positivity of a specific operator, showing it commutes with the Grauert invariant. This formula enables us to prove the Grauert tube is a domain of holomorphic automorphisms for $t > I$.

We introduce MARINLINGA, a novel algorithm designed to efficiently calculate the reverse line graph of a given graph G. This computation involves transforming G into a new graph, denoted as G^, such that a well-established graph theoretical connection exists between G and G^. Specifically, a edge in G is mapped to a vertex in G^ and vice versa. MARINLINGA has been rigorously tested on a large dataset of 1199 real-world graphs, yielding optimal performance in terms of speed and reduced memory consumption. Notably, MARINLINGA exhibits a time complexity of O(nm) and memory consumption of O(m) for the output.

This note examines the connection between roots related to free energy minimization in planar curves and real Schur roots in quivers, with a focus on non-self-intersecting curves. We demonstrate that for a quiver lacking cycles, the associated roots coincide with real Schur roots, establishing a relationship that can be interpreted as a dual relationship between roots and real Schur roots, with curve perturbations mirroring mutations in the quiver.

In application maintenance, developers often encounter issues stemming from bloated dependencies, which are unnecessary components or code that have become entangled in a project's dependencies and often result in maintenance difficulties. To address this, a study has been conducted to investigate the characteristics of bloated dependencies in open-source Java projects. By analyzing 51 Java repositories on GitHub using static analysis, the researchers identified 1,116 bloated dependencies, which were then categorized based on their age, scope, and language. A comparison of these characteristics with a control group of 200 dependencies revealed key findings, including the correlation between bloated dependencies and specific package types, the prevalence of their presence in certain projects, and the influence of dependency management tools on their size. These insights offer a foundation for future research to address the problem of bloated dependencies.

The amount of shared ancestry between two segments of a polymer chain formed by non-ideal polymer chains is calculated, along with an approximate formula for calculating this value when the segments are located far apart, up to a logarithmic correction. This formula is then used to analyze how shared ancestry affects the behavior of a polymer chain in two different scenarios: when two points on the same chain are considered, and when considering the self-similarity of the chain due to its repeating units. When self-similarity is taken into account, the sequence of numbers describing the size of the polymer chain segments exhibits a scaling pattern that changes from an inverse relationship to a logarithmic correction.

A key aspect of multistage distributionally robust optimization is to generate scenario paths that align with the probability distribution of the stochastic variables. These sequence of scenarios are used to create a conditional probability distribution in the next decision stage, contingent on prior outcomes. We introduce a novel optimization problem to efficiently calculate these sequence of scenarios, based on dynamic programming, with the ability to utilize k-means clustering for rapid computation at the cost of the number of clusters k, within a polynomial time complexity. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through numerical results for a multistage wind power forecasting problem.

This paper introduces a novel approach to temporal action detection, where we leverage a recurrent neural network (RNN) to generate and combine feature representations of future actions with those of past actions, enabling more accurate prediction of future actions. Our proposed network architecture, referred to as the Future Reference RNN (RefRNN), has been successfully tested and evaluated on two benchmark datasets for temporal action localisation, including the ActivityNet-1.3 and THUMOS-53 datasets, with our results demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods in terms of temporal action detection.

In this study, we examine deep thermalization in highly complex quantum systems, 
specifically through the lens of a theory that extends a concept of randomizing 
matrix multiplication to operate on a large number of particles. The theoretical 
framework of random unitary circuits offers a means to study the rapid exchange 
of energy among numerous particles and our analysis demonstrates that it fulfills 
certain precise expectations for achieving deep thermalization. Furthermore, 
by applying the theory to a model consisting of many interacting conserved 
quantities, we have found that thermalization can be measured using the 
behavior of a specific observable, and we have also found evidence of the impact 
of these interactions on the rate of thermalization.

We establish criteria for the boundedness of pseudo-differential operators on homogeneous trees, derived from a Hardy space dualization process. Using these criteria, we generate a comprehensive class of weighted Hardy space Hardy spaces. This yields new bounded criteria for various types of homogeneous tree operators and, as a result, we are able to reprove the boundedness of classical operators such as the Kakeya operator and the Riesz transform without relying on prior function decomposition.

The increasing presence of smartphones in households and the advancement of 5G technology have heightened concerns about the potential electromagnetic field effects on users. To address these concerns, we performed a 12-month exposure monitoring study of 5G electromagnetic field exposure in Finland, analyzing data for 21 random sampling points and 18 residential locations. Our results showed that, on average, users' exposure levels were significantly lower than those emitted by their devices. More importantly, we found that, on average, users' exposure levels are also lower than those emitted by their devices. Our analysis further revealed a very low correlation between user exposure and usage levels across all 21 sampling points. These findings suggest that, to a significant degree, users' exposure levels are lower than those emitted by their devices, and the duration of user device usage has a minimal impact.

Deep neural networks often produce inaccurate predictions with excessive confidence on data that lies outside the trained dataset domain, highlighting the need for methods that can accurately detect such out-of-distribution (OD) samples. Our novel approach, CODEs, uses self-attention mechanisms to identify and quantify the differences between OD samples and in-distribution data, thereby providing more reliable probability estimates for OD samples. By incorporating a single additional self-attention layer into the network, our method demonstrates improved accuracy in identifying OD samples and estimating their likelihood. Our experiments show that this approach produces more accurate probability estimates for OD samples compared to existing methods, while also showcasing enhanced robustness against common adversarial attacks.

The study of azimuthal correlations between a jet and a high-transverse-momentum Z boson offers insight into the probe jet's quark flavor and is also highly sensitive to little-scattered initial particles in high-energy collisions. This study presents data from proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV energy cross-checked against various theoretical models that account for the impact of the second-order perturbation theory and parton shower processes. The analysis focuses on central $Z$ boson rapidity and high-transverse-momentum jets within specific rapidity and transverse-momentum ranges, with a 50 GeV threshold for the boson and a 30 GeV transverse-momentum threshold for the jets. The data are compared to the predictions from Monte Carlo generators and parton showers, with a particular emphasis on their ability to accurately replicate the observed correlations. The analysis also includes a comparison of the data to the calculations based on fixed-order perturbative quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order precision.

The primary objective of this research paper is to develop a comprehensive understanding of semi-supervised and unsupervised deep learning models that utilize complex graphical structures. To achieve this, we first provide an in-depth analysis of the existing knowledge in these areas and then introduce a novel two-stage approach that streamlines the model training process. This proposed method streamlines the process of training deep neural networks by eliminating the need for the gradient descent algorithm. Notably, this approach can be applied to self-training, temporal ensembling, and mean teacher methods, effectively simplifying their implementation and enhancing their performance. To further demonstrate its efficacy, we conducted an extensive review of the most effective models in several prominent datasets and then integrated our method to enhance their performance. This integrated approach not only simplifies the implementation of existing methods but also significantly improves their performance.

Our proposed method, called Multi-View Federated Outlier Detection (MFOD), is designed for detecting unusual data patterns across multiple feeds and different types of edge devices. Building on the concept of training a neural network to produce a vector of errors, we have created a new input representation that incorporates these error vectors. The resulting feature set is then used in a federated learning framework to train a One-Class Support Vector Machine (SVM) on the aggregated features. The MFOD method has been tested using real-world and synthetic data, and has shown a significant improvement in detecting outliers compared to existing approaches. The code for this research is available in an online repository.

This paper examines a nonlinear equation in Banach spaces that incorporates hysteresis, demonstrating the equation has a singular mild solution which is uniquely defined and becomes classical under specific conditions defined by an inequality based on the constants from the resolvent family and the Banach space's measure of non-compactness.

We examine the possibility of neutrino-photon interactions facilitated by a light
(pseudo)scalar mediator. This potential interaction can be caused by a coupling between
the mediator and neutrinos, as well as a coupling between a photon and a vector mediator that
forms a pseudoscalar operator. We investigate the constraints on these couplings from
electromagnetic experiments and show that they can be very stringent. We also consider the
possibility of observable signals in experimental searches for neutrino-photon interactions.
Furthermore, we propose a new method for searching for neutrino-photon interactions using
high-energy neutrinos in ice and the Earth.

The significance of glial cell involvement in the brain's neural activity has long been recognized, particularly in the synchronization and regulation of neural networks. However, the direct impact of these interactions on the learning and inference processes within artificial neural networks has not been thoroughly explored. This study aims to investigate the effect of incorporating a glial component into deep learning networks, which could potentially lead to a glial-based learning framework that adapts to the learning rate in a more efficient manner. Furthermore, the proposed framework seeks to minimize the potential negative consequences of glial involvement, such as a decrease in learning stability.

In a magnetic vortex field, a spin-1/2 particle moving through a double-slit barrier exhibits the double-slit interference effect. Our findings demonstrate the presence of entanglement between internal and external degrees of freedom for this particle. We've also identified a transition in the interference pattern as we adjust the resonance condition for the external degree of freedom, indicating non-closure of the spacetime for this particular type of particle.

We explore the likelihood of a Brownian particle reaching a moving boundary before staying away from it forever. This scenario is applicable in both biological and physical contexts. To analyze it, we examine the motion of a particle mean-field model with boundaries shifting in time. By setting the two time scales, n and N, we can identify the movement of the boundary over a short period (n) and the duration before the particle is trapped (N). This study reveals that the behavior of the particle is influenced by both time scales. It is also discovered that the particle's probability of reaching the boundary for the nth time scales with a power law of time, while its trapping time scales with a power law of time raised to a fractional exponent. Furthermore, it was found that the particle's escape rate is influenced by two competing time scales, which can lead to a trapping trap effect.

For a type of knot known as an L-space knot, its Alexander polynomial is used to define the formal semigroup within the knot torsion-free module, specifically $x^{-A(L)(x)}\mathcal{T}_S$. It is proven that this semigroup is always geometric if the knot is tightly tight, and we determine the specific conditions under which $x^{-A(L)(x)}\mathcal{T}_S$ is closed under addition.

This study explores the kinetic theory of many-particle systems, specifically focusing on the Boltzmann equation's semigroup and its application to the inviscid limit of fluid dynamics. We examine how this theory can be used to study the evolution of a fluid's velocity potential, with a particular emphasis on its Vlasov-type flow. Building upon the work of Villani, we reevaluate and reinterpret it for the kinetic BGK model, and then generalize the findings to the kinetic BGK-Maxwell model. This allows us to demonstrate the convergence of the kinetic model to the Euler equation in the inviscid limit, and obtain a rate of convergence for the kinetic model's solution.

In this study, we introduce an advanced deep-learning based method for identifying objects in two-dimensional images, specifically from the perspective of remote sensing. Our approach combines the strengths of deep neural networks, using a method called ensemble deep-learning, in order to significantly improve overall performance. A novel method for generating training samples, known as the instance-subset technique, is also presented. Our proposed ensemble deep-learning based method (called ESDN) incorporates the principles of deep networks, specifically the YOLO-V3 and EfficientNet architectures, along with a strategy for adjusting model weights based on uncertainty. Additionally, a technique called instance-subset is employed to generate training samples. Our method was tested using the well-known U-2 dataset and demonstrated superior performance compared to comparable techniques.

Code can often be identified by its underlying structure, yet this can be distorted by renaming and refactoring. To analyze coding behavior, researchers focus on identifying identifiers that differ from their typical counterparts. To this end, this study develops a method to recognize and categorize these identifiers. To train this system, a substantial dataset was created by gathering identifiers from 1,000 top-rated GitHub projects. This collection was analyzed to understand naming conventions and patterns across different types of identifiers. By comparing these patterns to standard naming practices, the difference in these identifiers can be quantified. To test the reliability of this method, a series of experiments were conducted using a code editor plugin that can suggest and apply name standardizations.

Let $\mathbb{F}$ be an arbitrary field and $q$ a non-zero element within it, with the field of $q$-rational numbers defined as $\mathbb{Q}(q)$. We create a $q^2$-dimensional unital associative algebra, denoted $A(q), $ with a basis $\{x, y, z, u\}$ and define operations through relations: $x^2y^2 = y^2x^2,$ $xyy = yxy + x^2y^2,$ $yzu + zyu = zzz + zyu,$ and $zuz = zuz + zzz.$ We then identify the nilpotent vectors within this algebra as $N(q) = \{nu : n \in \mathbb{N}, n \geq 2, n \in \mathbb{Z}, nu \in A(q)\}$ and investigate nilpotent ideal-likes within $A(q),$ denoted as $I(q) = \{a \in A(q) : ax + ax \in N(q)\}$ for which we prove $I(q)$ is an ideal within $A(q).$ Furthermore, we establish the structure of $I(q)$ and show $A(q)/I(q)$ has the same algebraic properties as $A(q).$ We also demonstrate that the quotient $A(q)/I(q)$ contains a one-dimensional subal

The primary goal of this research is to develop a comprehensive mathematical framework for modeling the evolution of grain structure in multiphase polycrystalline materials during thermal treatment. The framework is specifically designed to accommodate complex microstructures, such as those found in materials like stainless steel. The model is based on a system of partial differential equations that describe the changes in grain size and composition within each individual grain. It takes into account how the internal boundaries between grains shift over time, as well as the interactions between the individual grains. The model was validated by comparing its predictions to the actual microstructures of heat-treated stainless steel samples and showed a strong correlation. The model was also used to investigate how different heat treatment processes affect the microstructures of these materials. The results indicated that, in certain conditions, the microstructures can evolve through a series of transformations from a single phase to multiple phases. Additionally, the model found that, under specific conditions, the changes in grain size follow a common pattern in all grains within a polycrystalline material.

We present a novel approach that enhances the accuracy and robustness of 3D human pose and shape prediction by leveraging a large database of annotated human models. The quality of a training dataset is vital in training reliable models. Our method optimizes the distribution of training labels through active learning, utilizing a multi-armed bandit technique to focus on the most informative samples. By doing so, it maximizes the accuracy benefit while minimizing annotation costs. The method is particularly effective in addressing the challenge of estimating human pose and shape from diverse human poses in diverse environments with limited training data. Our approach is demonstrated to outperform the current state-of-the-art methods on the Human3.6M benchmark.

In a dilute system of $d$-wave electrons with a small number of centers exhibiting opposite attractive forces (known as U-centers or attractive interactions), superconductivity arises.  The origin of this superconductivity is a result of the attractive interactions combined with the strong repulsive forces between the electrons.  A key factor contributing to this superconductivity is the ability of electrons to form temporary pairs with other electrons.  A crucial aspect of this superconductivity is its insensitivity to the presence of an additional unbalanced force acting on the electrons, with the critical temperature remaining unchanged even in the presence of such a force.  The origin of this unbalanced force is a result of an imbalance in the distribution of attractive interactions, with some centers exhibiting stronger and weaker attractive forces than others.  The insensitivity of the superconductivity to the unbalanced force is a result of a balance between the attractive interactions and the repulsive forces acting on the electrons.  The origin of this balance is a result of the strong repulsive forces acting on the electrons, with the strong repulsive forces acting as a 'cushion' to absorb the unbalanced force.  The study of this superconductivity has implications for the understanding of superconductivity in real materials, with the origin of this superconductivity providing a new perspective on how superconductivity arises in these materials.

We introduce a single extension of the Standard Model, which includes a single scalar leptoquark and a non-standard fermion, to study its implications for high-energy processes at the LHC. The new particles' interactions with the standard model's fermions and leptons are represented by a unified Lagrangian. Theoretical bounds on leptoquark mass are derived from the constraints of unobserved particle decay and the requirement that the new particles not exceed the LHC's detected particle mass limits. A detailed numerical analysis of the stable particles' production and decays is conducted, focusing on the relationships between lepton flavor and the lepton-quark correlations. The study's results are presented in terms of the physical quantities of the lepton quark mass, lepton quark mixing parameter, and the ratio of the lepton quark coupling to the standard model's fermions. The work's implications for the LHC's upcoming Run III are discussed in detail.

Machine learning has become a multifaceted field that incorporates insights and techniques from multiple disciplines. Over the past decade, category theory has been applied to machine learning, influenced by concepts in homotopy type theory and algebraic geometry. This application has been particularly successful in understanding the global properties of machine learning models, offering a structural and compositional approach that complements traditional techniques. In this survey, we explore the growing intersection of category theory and machine learning by examining the current progress and future directions in this field.

This paper explores the concept of dynamic terminal sliding mode control in the context of second- and third-order motion systems. To achieve this, the paper utilizes the concept of dynamic control parameters that replace discrete terminal control actions. A novel non-adiabatic control action is introduced, which eliminates the requirement for infinite gain coefficients. A new sliding mode control parameter is developed, ensuring zero error convergence in finite time for the error and its derivative. To validate the proposed approach, the paper analyzes second- and third-order motion systems, determining the optimal power allocation of measurable output states for second-order Newton's motion dynamics at 0.5 and third-order motion dynamics at 0.33, respectively. Furthermore, the paper provides a Lyapunov stability analysis to demonstrate that the control system is stable in the sense of Lyapunov.

Lithium-ion batteries are crucial components in numerous devices and systems that rely on renewable energy. To ensure optimal performance and safety, thorough characterization of these batteries is essential, particularly during manufacturing and usage. Researchers have developed non-invasive techniques to examine lithium-ion batteries' internal structures and state of health. Using these techniques, they studied various factors such as thickness, intercalability, and degradation levels of individual battery components within complete cells and after cycling. Results from both methods showed consistent trends and validated each other. Quantitative information from one method enabled the other method, demonstrating its potential to enhance data interpretation and accuracy. Further analysis revealed that the electrode thickness measured by X-ray methods correlated linearly with the electrode's surface area. These findings highlight the effectiveness of non-invasive characterization techniques in informing decisions on battery manufacturing processes and managing battery health in applications and services.

This study presents a discrete-time approach to tracking control of a gantry crane under real-world conditions. Unlike the traditional method, which relies on continuous time and discrete time for analysis and control, respectively, the proposed approach uses a discrete-time model with a reduced state dimension to simplify system dynamics and replace the traditional continuous-time controller. A discrete-time state-space controller is then designed using a Lyapunov stability function to demonstrate the system's stability and fast convergence properties. Through simulations in C++ and comparisons with the classic continuous method, it is shown that the discrete-time approach can effectively control the gantry crane while the classic method fails.

We've developed a comprehensive dataset of 2.2 million captions for 1.1 million images extracted automatically and enhanced through human editing. This massive dataset, referred to as ALR4K, is now available alongside two smaller parallel English-French and English-Spanish datasets, totaling 1.1 million data points in each language pair. This study presents an in-depth analysis of the evolution of the English dataset from its initial 300K state to its current 2.2 million size. We also provide a detailed breakdown of the costs associated with human revisions and the cross-lingual enhancement processes. In addition, we have conducted extensive experiments with three distinct image captioning systems, evaluating performance on different subsets of the English dataset in various training and testing configurations.

Two disjoint sets $A$ and $B$ form a well-connected pair of strings if any permutation of their union results in a string with $A$ and $B$ intertwined throughout.  A collection of strings is well-connected if any two strings within it create well-connected pairs.  The well-connected well-character string parameter is the minimum number of strings from a set $S$, consisting of $n$ strings, that are well-connected.  The paper investigates the well-connected well-character parameter, deriving an $O(n^2)$ algorithm and proving a lower bound of $|S|^{2/3-\epsilon}$ on its value.  Building upon previous work by Bousquet, Ferragina, and Vries that established a lower bound of $|S|^{1/2-\epsilon}$, the paper's upper bound is the first non-polynomial lower bound known to be proven for parameterization by the size of $S$.

Ehresmann semigroups can be considered as a broader category that includes generalized inverse semigroups, encompassing all bijective Ehresmann semigroups and their subcategories. Building on this concept, we can define and examine ordered Ehresmann semigroups, demonstrating their fundamental characteristics and discussing their applications in the context of ordered semigroup theory.

Recent self-attention architectures exhibit a notable trade-off between depth and layer width. Contrary to initial design principles, we challenge this relationship and demonstrate that depth and layer width are not mutually exclusive. By revisiting the attention mechanism, we establish a theoretical foundation to support the effective utilization of full-width attention heads. This foundation is implemented through the attention block, a novel component that can replace existing attention heads. The attention block enables the reduction of layer width at any point within a neural network, without compromising its expressiveness, according to empirical evidence from various tasks. Furthermore, we introduce a simple rescaling method to enhance the quality of generated subspaces, thereby facilitating the reuse of attention heads. This approach is empirically verified through experiments on standard computer vision and natural language processing tasks, including image classification, object detection, language modeling, and machine translation.

BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles synthesized at 160 $^{\circ}$C exhibit a R- phase structure and exhibit enhanced photocatalytic activity when used to degrade various pollutants. Compared to bulk BiFeO$_{3}$ and BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles synthesized at 300 $^{\circ}$C with N- and R-phases respectively, the low-temperature nanoparticles demonstrate superior performance under both visible and UV light. This improved functionality is attributed to their small size and high surface area. The results suggest that these nanoparticles could serve as an efficient visible-driven catalyst for the degradation of pollutants.

A new, comprehensive framework is introduced for the study of radiative electroweak symmetry breaking within an extension of the Standard Model, where two Higgs doublets are present. The model is characterized by a specific condition, under which only one Higgs doublet develops a non-zero vacuum expectation value. The proposed framework is compatible with current experimental findings and offers a straightforward method for accounting for radiative corrections to the electroweak scale. The model's properties are thoroughly examined, including its implications for the Higgs boson masses, its impact on precision electroweak measurements, and its potential for new physics beyond what's observable at the LHC. The model's predictions for the Higgs boson production cross-sections are also evaluated.

In computer vision, predicting the contents of a box based on an image of a hand holding an object is a complex problem that has practical applications in robotics and everyday life. Most current methods require at least two images: one with the object being held and another with the hand in different positions. The issue with this approach is that it's difficult to obtain these images simultaneously. The goal of this research is to propose a novel method that can achieve comparable results with just a single image of the hand holding the object. To address this problem, the proposed method focuses on capturing the movement of the hand and its impact on the object being held. The proposed method utilizes a combination of a hand pose estimation network and a 3D reconstruction network to jointly learn the movement of the hand and reconstruct the object being held. The proposed method also employs a 3D pose estimation network to estimate the movement of the object being held. The proposed method is evaluated on a custom dataset consisting of 100,000 images of the contents of a box with the object being held in different positions. The results show that the proposed method achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art method, even when trained on a small dataset. The proposed method also shows that the movement of the hand is crucial in accurately reconstructing the object being held. The proposed method is also shown to be effective in cases where the hand movement is not visible. The proposed method also shows that the movement of the object being held is not crucial in this problem

The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array's (ALMA) system is capable of detecting the Sun's magnetic fields through a technique that utilizes the spectropolarimetry of solar features. Specifically, the Ca-K line is used to identify the solar photosphere's magnetic properties. Our research involved simulating the spectropolarimetric behavior of the Sun and analyzing how ALMA can observe it with the aid of the instrument's polarimetry. We discovered that the Equal Contrast technique significantly improves the correlation between alfa and Ca-K intensity by adjusting the instrument's response to changing solar conditions on different wavelengths. Our findings suggest that the Equal Contrast method effectively reconstructs the solar Ca-K line shape and intensity, even when accounting for the instrument's limitations. We also found that the instrument's polarimetry has a minimal impact on the solar magnetic fields measured across the Ca-K line profile.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays has been conducted using LHCb data from 3 fb^-1 of proton-proton collisions at energies of 7 and 8 TeV. No significant excess over background was observed, and an upper limit on the branching fraction was established as 9 times ten to the negative 9 powers, valid at the 95% confidence level. This new result significantly reduces the discrepancy between predictions made by different theoretical models. Furthermore, the observed number of events of $\Sigma^+ \to p e^+ e^-$ was in agreement with $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay yields and in line with a $\Sigma^+ \to p \gamma$ branching fraction of 0.00011 (with an uncertainty of 0.00007).

A key challenge in distributed Symbolic Execution is effectively utilizing available processing units. Existing methods primarily rely on one of two approaches: one approach sends distinct types of messages between servers, while the other employs virtual machines to handle different stages of the analysis. However, these strategies have a significant limitation, as they require a clear division of tasks, making it difficult to handle statements with complex structures. To address this issue, we present an innovative solution, which is based on one unit's ability to process and analyze a portion of a statement, sending only relevant data to other units and retaining local information for future use. This strategy is referred to as Test-Depth Partitioning, as it enables a server to send only relevant data to other units and utilize local information for future use. We have implemented this approach in a distributed SE framework, which is capable of efficiently handling complex statements, is highly scalable, and offers a high degree of flexibility when it comes to message types.

The magnetic relaxation data of magnetic nanoparticles is represented by the magnetic monopole approximation, which simplifies complex dipolar interactions. Our research shows that this approximation effectively models the relaxation of highly disordered magnetic nanoparticle systems, consisting of particles ranging from 20 nanometers to 800 nanometers in diameter and with a wide range of ratios of particle diameter to magnetic core diameter. We found that the magnetic relaxation time is influenced by the ratio of particle diameter to magnetic core diameter and the strength of dipolar interactions, but the shape of the relaxation curve remains consistent. Our findings align with simulations of magnetization dynamics and experimental data on magnetic nanoparticle assemblies. Our study provides a practical method for simulating the magnetic relaxation of weakly interacting nanoparticle systems and suggests that relaxation time is more sensitive to particle size than magnetic core size.

A rising concern in machine learning, federated learning has gained significance due to its ability to safeguard data while maintaining learning accuracy. This paper presents a novel federated learning framework specifically designed for outdoor environmental monitoring, where weather conditions are classified using smartphone-based federated learning. An experimental setup was established to gather real-world weather data, and an federated learning model incorporating CNN architecture was developed. This classification model was thoroughly tested on diverse weather conditions and evaluated for both accuracy and learning dynamics.

Recent neural network-based approaches have achieved impressive success in short text classification tasks. However, they often rely on complex recurrent neural networks that can be difficult to train and require a substantial number of parameters. This paper proposes a novel, state-based recurrent neural network architecture that utilizes a finite state machine to model text sequences, thereby significantly reducing parameter overhead and training requirements. This approach is particularly beneficial for short text classification tasks. Furthermore, it proposes a dynamic state machine framework that can learn to replicate long-term text sequences, and it includes a training speed analysis to demonstrate the efficiency of its state-based design. Experimental results show that this approach can achieve comparable or even superior performance to existing methods while requiring significantly fewer parameters and training time.

Our research delves into how changes in the thickness and temperature affect
the performance of Fabry-Pérot etalons. The wave-optics framework, which
predicts the interference pattern's intensity and location of maxima and minima,
is used to calculate the electric field. By using the phase difference between
the fields inside the etalon and its two ends, we can represent the electric
field, which is independent of the etalon's thickness. We analyze the etalon's
sensitivity to thickness variations, taking into account the refractive index and
temperature dependencies, and derive a simplified yet comprehensive formula
describing the electric field's sensitivity. This novel formula enables the
design of etalons with reduced optical thickness sensitivity. This could be
particularly useful for creating etalons that operate at different
temperatures or are exposed to varying levels of air thickness. We validate
our findings through simulations and experiments on etalons with different
thicknesses and wavelengths.

Given two labeled sets of n points, $S$ and $T$, which are convex and disjoint, we have a bijection $\sigma$ mapping $S$ to $T$. A matching is considered compatible if it doesn't violate this mapping for any points. A compatible matching of $S$ and $T$ can have at most $\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil$ edges. However, when both sets are unlabeled, we can find sets that prevent a matching with more than $\lceil\frac{n^2+3}{6}\rceil$ edges. Furthermore, we can prove that with both labeled sets being convex, we can find sets $S$ and $T$ that prevent a matching with more than $\frac{3n}{5}+O(\sqrt{n})$ edges.

The emergence of emerging technologies such as 3D integration for performance, security, and scalability has driven the development of complex systems with numerous integrated components. Consequently, designing and verifying these systems at the pre-fabrication stage is becoming increasingly difficult. To address these challenges, a new approach to system design and verification is needed, focusing on modular, reconfigurable architectures composed of interconnected software-defined units. This approach is exemplified in modular, monolithic die configurations known as 'chiplets,' where functional components and interconnected networks are integrated on a single wafer-fabricated die. To facilitate this vision, a novel architectural framework is proposed, combining reconfigurable computing and interconnect technologies into a single module. This framework is designed to simplify the process of integrating and verifying modular systems composed of multiple chiplets from the same or different vendors. To validate this concept, a proof-of-concept chiplet system was designed and implemented on a custom hardware platform, utilizing a reconfigurable network-on-chip and co-design methodology. This implementation demonstrates the feasibility of this approach and enables the development of modular, secure systems composed of multiple interconnected chiplets from the same or different vendors.

A common approach in survival analysis is the mixture cure model, used to estimate the portion of the population that remains unaffected by a potential risk factor. The model distinguishes between individuals who are initially at risk and those who develop the risk over time. The goal of this study is to develop a new approach to estimating a specific type of parameter in the mixture cure model. The parameter of interest is called the relative risk parameter and is calculated for subpopulations where the risk increases with time. The proposed method is a two-stage approach that uses maximum likelihood estimation and is more straightforward than existing methods, with the added benefit of providing standard error estimates. The new method was tested using simulated data and real-world datasets and compared to other existing approaches, with the results showing its effectiveness.

The nonlocal metric dimension of a graph, defined as the smallest set of vertices that can differentiate any two vertices based on their proximity to neighboring vertices, is studied. Specific examples include trees, unicyclic graphs, and grid graphs. It is observed that determining the nonlocal metric dimension for certain well-known structures can be complex, such as complete bipartite graphs and Kneser graphs. Further analysis provides upper and lower bounds for diameter-based dimensions of power graphs of cyclic groups.

In-memory computing systems have shown significant promise in efficiently executing Deep Neural Networks due to their ability to perform computations at the memory level, thus mitigating the issue of ever-growing data and energy consumption. However, these systems face challenges with non-linear activations such as ReLU due to the requirement for analog devices that closely replicate the digital non-linear function. To address this limitation, this study proposes a novel in-memory computing method that incorporates digital processing in conjunction with analog computation for Maximal Absolute Value (MAV) non-linear function. The MAV unit is implemented both digitally and in analog form, with simulation results indicating that the analog MAValon device performs similarly to a 45nm CMOS CMOS-based MAValon unit.

A new approach to constructing polar codes, referred to as shortened polar codes, is introduced and applied to polarisation kernels with reduced size but preserved complexity. This research proposes an algorithm for the design and analysis of these shortened large polarisation kernels, and validates their performance by implementing them in a custom lossless polar code decoder designed for integration with existing polar codes. The results demonstrate that the polar codes, specifically the A6 and A8 shortened large polarisation kernels, outperform both the DS and PS polar codes, and are suitable for integration with other polar codes, further improving their performance.

Seismic data contamination originates from diverse sources and poses a significant challenge to interpreters, necessitating time-consuming manual editing to rectify. Recent studies have leveraged deep learning techniques for data cleaning, but these methods are limited by the need for extensive training datasets and supervision. These requirements hinder the practical application of deep learning in real-world settings. In response, this study presents a novel unsupervised deep learning approach for removing noise from seismic datasets, leveraging a generative adversarial network (GAN). By utilizing a GAN, noise can be effectively eradicated from seismic data without the need for training data, significantly reducing computational requirements. Furthermore, this method can be easily adapted to address diverse data types. Experimental findings indicate that this proposed GAN approach outperforms conventional techniques, such as 2D wavelet and non-local means denoising algorithms, in terms of efficiency and effectiveness.

The observation of charge asymmetry through electron-positron pair polarization in lepton-ludlum scattering serves as a key tool to investigate the two-photon exchange effect. By analyzing data collected by the OLYMPUS collaboration with a substantial sample of events, a detailed examination of the interaction can be performed. The main focus lies in the analysis of the data using specific criteria to reach a definitive conclusion. The investigation into the two-photon exchange effect has been conducted in two distinct approaches: the first involves the analysis of the data based on the entire kinematic range, while the second focuses on a more confined area. The outcomes of the two approaches are compared to assess their consistency with each other.

A model of an antiferromagnetic lattice with electrons or holes that have been doped, and which are subject to on-site Coulomb interactions, is investigated. This system is mathematically formulated using a lattice version of a double-time thermal correlator, specifically for a doped electron or hole added to a quantum antiferromagnet. Utilizing the inhomogeneous Bethe-Salpeter equation a comprehensive quantum mechanical description is developed which elucidates the behavior of the system at long times. Furthermore, this framework is applied to a specific case where the doped electron or hole is inserted at a large distance from the background antiferromagnet. Under these conditions, this framework is shown to be consistent with the concept of a quasi-particle lifetime which decays exponentially with time.

Researchers studying various applications aim to identify the impact of independent variables on dependent variables and understand the intermediary processes in between. In multiple fields like epidemiology and social studies, achieving this understanding is essential. A widely accepted analytical framework for this purpose is mediation analysis, a statistical method that assesses the effects of independent variables on intermediate and final dependent variables. In this two-stage process, commonly used frequentist methods are vulnerable to finite sample biases and often rely on untestable linear assumptions. To address these limitations, this study presents two novel approaches based on bootstrap simulations. The first approach, called Bootstrap Mediation Property Testing, utilizes bootstrapping to estimate the confidence intervals of mediation property transformations. The second approach, called Bootstrap Mediation Property Estimation, simulates confidence intervals for mediation property transformations using bootstrapping. The performance of these methods is compared to existing frequentist methods and alternative bootstrap simulations-based methods in multiple experiments. The results show that both of these new approaches demonstrate superior performance compared to existing methods and are more robust against untested assumptions and linear models assumptions.

A starshade is an optical system designed to block light from a star, allowing for the creation of an artificial "dark field" where telescopes can take images or collect data without the star's influence. We describe the concept of a deployable, external starshade system consisting of an opaque mask and a light-scattering screen that telescopes can utilize to measure light levels in the dark field. The analysis includes a detailed mathematical model that calculates the starlight flux and the star's image point in the dark field, taking into account the large outer phase plate of the starshade. We also provide a simplified model of the starshade that is useful for estimating its performance and resolving the underlying mathematical challenges.

The detection of suicidal intent is a critical public health concern, yet current research has limitations in transferring to the general population due to overfitting. Machine learning holds promise in identifying at-risk individuals earlier, potentially saving lives. However, real-world deployment requires careful evaluation of machine learning models using both clinical and machine learning metrics. In this study, we introduce a set of tools for evaluating machine learning models detecting suicidal content, specifically focusing on out-of-sample risk prediction. Our analysis involves training and testing various models detecting suicidal content, examining their performance on an independent dataset, and evaluating their predictive capabilities. Our results indicate that the suicidal content detection models exhibit moderate to good performance within the dataset, but their ability to predict risk in the wider population is significantly lower.

Building upon the concept of supersymmetric Schwarzians, we develop an action for a supersymmetric field in anti-de Sitter space and outline its associated Ward identities. This action serves as a foundation for a supersymmetric conformal field theory, ultimately leading to the characterization of superconformal groups within anti-de Sitter settings with various dimensions and signatures.

Currently, there is an abundance of research focusing on discrete dynamical systems, 
with their fundamental principles rooted in simple recurrence formulas. Due to their straightforward 
nature, researchers frequently examine the properties of their solutions in detail. 
This paper presents a new approach by introducing a set of rules to automatically generate 
recurrence formulas and explore their associated solution behaviors. 
With a unique combination of natural language processing and evolutionary computation, 
our proposed method can efficiently produce new recurrence formulas that exhibit 
intriguing solution behaviors. We validate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing 
it with conventional analytical methods, also providing potential educational benefits 
for instructors and students alike.

The nonlinear electrodynamics model known as the Born-Infeld theory has been used to analyze a specific type of wormhole geometry. This specific solution was derived from a modified version of the Born-Infeld model, with a metric defined as $f=\kappa r^b Q(r)$ and assumptions of a spherically symmetric spacetime and constant magnetic field B. This solution was obtained for a specific power parameter b > -2. The parameters k and Q in the solution represent the cosmological constant and non-linear electromagnetic charge respectively. The properties of the wormhole solution were investigated in detail for various values of the power parameter b.

Consider a linear function $\varphi$ with coefficients in a field $\mathbb{F}$, defined over a vector space $V$. A subset $A$ of $V$ is called a $\varphi$-Sidon set if it satisfies the condition $\sum_{\alpha\in A}\varphi(\alpha)=0$ implies \(\sum_{\alpha\in A}\chi(\alpha)v=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{F}\mathbb{S}_{m}}\chi(\alpha)v=0\) for all $v\in V$ and some $m\in\mathbb{N}$ where $\chi$ denotes a character of $\mathbb{F}_{m}$. The paper introduces a new approach to determining the smallest $m$ for which $A$ is $\varphi$-Sidon if it's an $m$-term Sidon set. The paper investigates properties of $\varphi$-Sidon sets in various contexts including finite fields, polynomial rings and linear codes.

In the context of a 1D quantum XY model, where vertices and edges are varied in proportion, the magnetic susceptibility is analyzed as temperature and disorder strength vary. At zero temperature, the model exhibits a phase transition from a non-singlet to a singlet ground state. Through a combination of field theory, numerical simulations, and exact models, we establish that the critical point of this transition is a random critical point that falls within the realm of the Yang-Lee edge singularity. Furthermore, we find that the magnetic susceptibility diverges in a non-mean-field manner at this critical point, and that this behavior is consistent across different temperature ranges, including both high and low temperatures. Additionally, we show that the susceptibility exhibits a finite value in the presence of strong disorder, and that this value grows in a non-algebraic manner with increasing temperature. The underlying cause of this behavior is attributed to the random nature of the vertices and edges, and is supported by a comparison with a related model featuring random domains.

We investigate the phenomenon of unusual activation in systems with variable uncertainty. This research explores the relationship between information theory and classical statistical mechanics through the concept of an information-equivalent classical gas. We use information-theoretic techniques to study the dynamics of Brownian particles and observe an anomalous activation effect in their behavior. We find that systems with higher initial temperatures or entropies have a greater tendency to equilibrate faster than systems with lower initial temperatures or entropies under specific conditions. Our findings in classical gases are then applied to a quantum harmonic chain and show that the information-equivalent particles of classical gases exhibit analogous unusual activation behavior.

The behavior of one-dimensional quasicrystals with power-law hopping is studied,
exhibiting a critical phase in the presence of interacting bosons, which is
investigated using the exact Bethe approximation. The impact of interactions on the
pairs in the system is analyzed using the superfluid fraction and pair fidelity,
showing that repulsive or attractive interactions have opposing effects. Furthermore,
the energy spectrum of the system is analyzed to assess the influence of
repulsiveness and attractiveness in the energy level distribution, with repulsive
interactions resulting in higher localization and larger energy gaps. These findings
are verified through the study of quantum state entanglement using the von Neumann
entropy.

Task-oriented dialogue systems have seen significant growth in recent years,
despite their current shortfalls. These systems predominantly focus on English and
Chinese languages, leaving many others unexplored. To overcome this limitation,
we introduce Dialauganet, a self-supervised unsupervised dialogue translation system.
This system can be easily extended to any bilingual pairs without language-specific
constraints. In our experiments, Dialauganet demonstrates impressive results, with a
state-of-the-art BLEU score of 13.28 and a 47.7% Character-2-Words BLEU score
on the ETU dataset for neural machine translation.

The pre-mRNA splicing process removes non-coding sequences from genes, reorganizing them for further use, however it's also associated with various diseases including cancer. We created an innovative method utilizing deep learning to identify alternative splicing events in the pre-mRNA splicing process. This method utilizes a graph convolutional neural network to analyze the splicing graph, where each node represents an exon/intron and is connected to its surrounding exons/introns. We compared our method to existing approaches including a S. major-specific model and four machine learning models. Our method demonstrated superior performance, achieving an accuracy of 92%, precision of 94%, F1 score of 0.8, and lower false discovery rates compared to other methods. Additionally, our method showed improved performance in predicting novel alternative splicing events.

The unique nature of the GDPR's data protection requirements is a key factor in its influence, as it emphasizes a risk-based approach that goes beyond Europe and requires a deep understanding of the broader global context. This leads to a pressing need for experts from various backgrounds, including data science, technology, law, and ethics, to work together to address the challenges of the 21st century. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current developments in the classification systems using machine learning and natural language processing, particularly in the context of identifying processing operations and assessing data protection impact assessments.

The three-dipole correlator approach has been successful in predicting the single 
inclusive particle production distribution for small values of the energy release. 
However, its applicability is yet to be explored for larger energy releases. In this 
research, we extend the approach to higher energies and find that it effectively 
predicts the shape of particle production for all energies, using parameters 
determined from smaller energy releases. Our findings are verified by comparing 
with experimental data on charged particle production in Pb-Pb collisions at a 
energy level of 2.76 TeV. Additionally, the approach is used to calculate the 
mean flow of particles and the ratio of their average momentum to the collision 
energy, yielding results in line with expectations.

The production of light nuclei in isobaric nuclear collisions is examined at the LHC using the TRENTO model. This model incorporates the coalescence and the statistical coalescence model, which represent the non-coalescence mechanism and the thermodynamic process respectively. Specifically, we've calculated the cross-sections for $\Lambda$, $\Lambda\bar{\Lambda}$, $d\bar{d}$, $^{3}H$, $^{3}\bar{H}$, $^{4}\text{He}$ and $^{5}\text{He}$ for both central and mid-rapidity collisions. This work is intended to provide a reference for the interpretation of experimental data collected by ALICE.

The majority of exoplanets discovered so far are likely to be surrounded by dense hydrogen-helium gas envelopes that have been stripped of their high temperatures and high pressure in their original form. The primary cause of this stripping is the intense atmospheric erosion that occurs when these planets orbit extremely close to their central stars. The process of this envelope formation and evolution is extremely complex, involving the interaction of both hydrodynamic and radiative transfer mechanisms, and is currently not well understood. The research presented in this study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by developing a new model that simulates the interaction of hydrodynamic and radiative transfer processes in the atmosphere of rocky exoplanets. The model, known as the Exo-Cloud model, is designed to be computationally efficient and can be used to analyze the properties of exoplanets in various stages of atmospheric stripping. The model's accuracy was tested through a series of simulations involving a range of rocky exoplanets with different atmospheric compositions and central temperatures. The results showed that the Exo-Cloud model is capable of accurately simulating the properties of exoplanets in various stages of atmospheric stripping. The model's findings were compared with those of other state-of-the-art models and showed that it can be used to analyze the properties of exoplanets in various stages of atmospheric stripping. The research presents the results of a comprehensive analysis of the properties of exoplanets in various stages of atmospheric stripping and discusses the implications of the model's findings for our understanding of their

A graph is said to be dispersable if it meets the conditions for a matching book thickness of k along with a maximum degree of k minus 1. This particular family of graphs is referred to as Q2k and features unique properties, encompassing planar subgraphs and cubicity. Notably, the Q2k graph set shares strong connections to the previously established family of snarks known as B2k. This paper delves into the structural properties of the Q2k family further by identifying edge-saturations that occur at specific degrees and the overall edge connectivity of the graph.

The importance of matrix inversion has been well-documented in various research studies.  While traditional methods of matrix inversion are often computationally complex, researchers have turned to iterative solutions for more efficient results.  This study presents a novel approach to matrix inversion using multilinear neural networks.  By utilizing an iterative method to minimize the error, we can find the solution to the problem, and our results show that this approach is highly resistant to the effects of noise.  Using this method, we can also find the local and global minimum of matrix inversion, and by adjusting the learning rate, we can control the speed of convergence.  Our research has far-reaching implications for a wide range of applications including signal processing, low-rank tensor identification, and fundamental multilinear neural networks.

In an inflationary model that combines ultra slow roll and ultra slow roll through a scalar field's double freeze-in process, we demonstrate that the curvature perturbations' evolution exhibits a notable change of slope. Consequently, the power spectrum is not solely dictated by the scale factor, but also influenced by the time evolution of the field's inflationary freeze-in. As a result, a novel approach is required to analyze the perturbations' statistical properties.

This research explores a complex optimization challenge known as refined assortment optimization, where advertisers must carefully curate display ads with multiple creative elements to maximize ad effectiveness and user relevance. The goal is to create a tailored set of advertising campaigns for each viewer, taking into account their individual preferences and ad variations. Building on previous research, which focused on a simplified assortment optimization problem where multiple ads are combined into a single unit, the refined assortment optimization problem models users' responses to individual ads more accurately and accounts for additional costs associated with ad rotation. We develop a new algorithm to tackle this problem, combining ideas from click maximization and budget allocation strategies, and evaluate its performance through experiments on real-world data, demonstrating significant improvements over current approaches.

In the context of time-to-event data, where the hazard rate often exhibits non-monotonic behavior, parametric regression models with flexible shapes can provide valuable insights. Traditional methods for estimating these models can be cumbersome due to complex calculations and limited inference tools. This paper introduces a Bayesian-based approach for estimating piecewise exponential hazard models using logistic functions, enabling the selection of model parameters via posterior distribution. Leveraging the Brownian motion's order statistics property, the resulting hazard function can be efficiently defined across different time intervals. Through simulated data analysis, the method showcases its competitive predictive capabilities. Its practical utility is further demonstrated in a real-world study of breast cancer, where the method is successfully utilized for the prediction of time-to-recurrence and time-to-death.

This article examines complex calculations required at the level of theoretical three-loop accuracy, in areas including electroweak, mixed electroweak-QCD, and supersymmetry. We delve into the history of these challenges and discuss key problems associated with their resolution. We also outline various approaches for addressing these difficulties, including the use of reduction, integration with the aid of tensors, and numerical methods. We then describe the progress made in the electroweak and mixed electewek-QCD sectors, and discuss the ongoing work on supersymmetry. We also highlight the work of several researchers who have contributed to the field and the projects they were involved in. We also outline our understanding of future research requirements. This report was initially prepared for an NSCL-NSCC workshop on Lattice-Loops, held at Michigan State University, USA, and was later revised for submission to the 2020 12th International Symposium on Lattice Hadron Physics and 5th Workshop on Lattice Field Theory in San Antonio, USA.

High-performance object storage solutions have emerged as a viable alternative to traditional file systems, particularly in high-performance computing (HPC) environments, offering faster data access and scalable storage. These object stores, however, often fall short in replicating and guaranteeing single-copy file guarantees, and their integration with HPC clusters necessitates complex configuration and tuning. Existing solutions require explicit handling of data locality and lack a clear integration framework. Our proposed SODA file system addresses these shortcomings by providing seamless file handling, automatic locality-based caching, and straightforward configuration. By leveraging object storage's inherent replication, SODA ensures the predictable consistency of single-copy file guarantees. Our evaluation on a large-scale distributed computing platform demonstrated SODA's performance advantages over traditional HPC file systems.

This paper explores a long-term pricing strategy for electric vehicle charging facilities designed to increase user satisfaction, reduce operational expenses, and minimize carbon emissions. A novel approach is presented, where the charging facilities are viewed as dynamic games with evolving demand and carbon emission goals. By establishing an optimal balance between user satisfaction and operational costs, the challenge of finding an optimal pricing function is addressed. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the optimal pricing function can be effectively approximated using a deep reinforcement learning approach, leading to improved user satisfaction, reduced operational costs, and decreased reliance on fossil fuels.

We prove the existence of Euclidean and Hermitian linear complementary dual (LCD) codes with different parameters within the Euclidean and Hermitian cases respectively. Further, we provide insights into Euclidean and Hermitian LCD codes with a single generator and explore their properties. The study also includes a detailed examination of binary LCD codes.

Building on a previously published paper [1], we revisit the calculation of
self-interlocking loops in general relativity and reframe the calculation by
focusing on a single type of wave function. This approach streamlines the
integration process and eliminates the need to convert wave packets. Furthermore,
we leverage the Poincaré algebra to simplify dimensional integration and
extract relevant scaling characteristics. This enables the discovery of
enlarged conservation laws through dimensional variation.

This study assesses the potential for a solar field development process in various regions of the American west, focusing on areas suitable for solar energy generation and transportation infrastructure. We integrate spatial data with economic and technical solar energy performance models to evaluate land suitability and competition factors. Our analysis reveals substantial potential for a solar field development pipeline in these regions, with significant implications for meeting regional energy demands and achieving a carbon-neutral electricity supply. Our results indicate that the most cost-effective solar energy portfolios, which supply 10% of the western states' electricity needs, can be established by combining 78% of the identified suitable sites, and 92% of the identified sites, without requiring substantial land reservations. Our research highlights the potential for a solar field development process in these regions to achieve a significant reduction in carbon emissions from electricity generation, and it also provides valuable insights into potential land use competition and mitigation strategies for large-scale land development projects.

It is recommended that novel vaccine trial designs be evaluated in light of the trial's objectives and that estimands be defined beforehand. We emphasize this notion and offer guidance on how these estimands should be developed for the time to event data collected in vaccine trials. We specifically focus on evaluating the vaccine's efficacy in hindering the development of symptoms, complications, and hospitalization due to a disease. We utilize proportional hazard modeling to examine both interim and final findings, as well as stratified data to account for factors like gender and baseline disease severity. We also explore how data collected on treatment arm participants, including healthy individuals, can be utilized in the trial. We provide examples of estimands that assess a treatment's capacity to prevent disease progression, symptoms, and treatment-related complications, while highlighting the challenges associated with evaluating vaccine efficacy against diseases with low incidence and infrequently occurring events.

This paper explores the spectral properties of normalized Laplacian in two types of network configurations: unweighted and weighted connections. Specifically, we derive expressions for the spectrum of a normalized Laplacian matrix of directed graphs under both unweighted and weighted scenarios. Additionally, we establish conditions to determine the multiplicity of the zero and the largest eigenvalues of the normalized Laplacian matrix. Furthermore, we identify a necessary condition for a normalized Laplacian matrix to be a primitive, which is directly linked to the communication network's topology.

In this paper, we explore a model of contextual linear bandits in a distributed framework. The framework consists of a teacher and k agents, with the teacher providing features and rewards for k elements in a d-dimensional space. The elements in this space are drawn from a Gaussian distribution and form the basis for contextual information. With no knowledge of the elements or their counts, agents must select actions to maximize the model's expected reward. The agents are restricted to a no communication, agent-teacher communication model where the teacher can only transmit information to agents, and agents can only send queries to the teacher. With a focus on this communication model, we derive new performance bounds for contextual linear bandits that improve upon previous results. The new bounds allow agents to perform with approximately 5d bits of information per context, achieving a significant improvement over previous bounds of O(d) bits per context. The new bounds also demonstrate that in a specific case where the teacher has limited information to transmit, agents can achieve a significant improvement over previous bounds, with an optimal performance that requires only a mere 1 bit per context.

The rapid advancement of machine learning algorithms has sparked widespread enthusiasm for their application in healthcare.
